presentingComplaint: Sudden transient right-arm weakness and slurred speech that fully resolved within 40 minutes
history: Witnessed abrupt onset of right upper-limb heaviness with difficulty gripping and mildly slurred speech while at breakfast this morning. Symptoms peaked immediately (no march or spread), lasted ~40 minutes, then resolved completely with no residual deficit. No headache, no loss of consciousness, no seizure activity, no positive visual phenomena. First such episode. PMH: hypertension (on amlodipine), type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, 30 pack-year ex-smoker. No prior stroke/TIA. Not on any antiplatelet or anticoagulant.
examination: Alert, fully orientated, GCS 15. Neurological examination now completely normal: power 5/5 all limbs, no dysarthria, no facial droop, no sensory or visual field deficit, gait normal. Right carotid bruit audible. No AF on cardiac auscultation (regular rhythm). No papilloedema. Pertinent negatives: no thunderclap headache, no meningism, no neck/eye pain, no focal deficit persisting at review.
imaging: Non-contrast CT head: no haemorrhage, no established infarct, no mass lesion. MRI-DWI (obtained urgently): no acute diffusion restriction (consistent with TIA rather than minor stroke). Carotid Doppler: 60-70% stenosis of the symptomatic left internal carotid artery.
finalDiagnosis: Transient ischaemic attack (high-risk, symptomatic carotid stenosis)
citations: Harrison 22e - Ischemic Stroke / Transient Ischemic Attack
AHA/ASA Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients with Stroke and TIA 2021
contraindications: Confirm no intracranial haemorrhage on imaging before starting antiplatelet therapy
Caution with dual antiplatelet therapy if active peptic ulcer or bleeding risk
Statin dose adjustment if hepatic impairment
edgeCases: Negative DWI does not exclude ischaemia - a true TIA has no infarct by definition, but minor stroke can mimic and mandates same urgent workup
Crescendo TIAs or ABCD2 high-risk features warrant admission
Must exclude hypoglycaemia and focal seizure as stroke mimics before labelling as TIA
expectedMaiK: Sudden focal neurological deficit that fully resolved with no acute infarct on DWI in a vasculopath is a transient ischaemic attack; this is a medical emergency carrying high early stroke risk, so urgent carotid imaging, antiplatelet therapy and risk-factor control are required.
expectedNextQuestions: What was the exact duration and did the deficit fully resolve?
Any atrial fibrillation, palpitations or known cardiac source?
Any preceding amaurosis fugax or prior similar episodes (crescendo pattern)?
expectedInvestigations: ECG and prolonged rhythm monitoring for atrial fibrillation

investigations: ECG and rhythm monitoring for atrial fibrillation
